p.src: Sima Zhao said to Shao Ti, an assistant in the Western Bureau, “The court officials all say that Shu cannot yet be attacked; this shows that their hearts are fearful. If they were forced to fight fiercely, they would surely be defeated. Now Zhong Hui alone has proposed the campaign against Shu, which shows that he is not afraid. Since he is unafraid, he is certain to destroy Shu. Once Shu is destroyed, the courage of its people will already be shattered. ‘A defeated general cannot speak of valor; a minister of a fallen state cannot plan for survival.’ Even if Zhong Hui should harbor rebellious ambitions, how could the people of Shu help him? As for the men of Wei, once victorious they will long to return home; they certainly will not follow Zhong Hui in revolt. There is even less cause to worry about them. This is known only to you and me. You must under no circumstances divulge it.” Shao Ti bowed in admiration.

p.src: Meanwhile, after Zhong Hui had finished making camp, he took his seat in the command tent and assembled all the generals to receive their orders. Among them were the army inspector Wei Guan and the protector-general Hu Lie; and the generals Tian Xu, Pang Hui, Tian Zhang, Yuan |, Qiu Jian, Xiahou Xian, Wang Jia, Huangfu Kai, Gou An, and more than eighty others. Zhong Hui said, “We need a great general to serve as vanguard, opening roads through the mountains and building bridges wherever he meets water. Who dares undertake it?” One man answered at once, “I am willing to go.” Zhong Hui looked and saw that it was Xu Yi, son of the fierce general Xu Chu. Everyone said, “No one but this man can serve as vanguard.” Zhong Hui summoned Xu Yi and said, “You are a general with a tiger’s frame and an ape’s arms, and both father and son are renowned. Now all the generals commend you as well. Take the seal of the vanguard, command five thousand cavalry and one thousand infantry, and advance directly upon Hanzhong. The army will be divided into three columns: you will lead the center through Xie Valley; the left column will pass through Luo Valley; and the right column through Ziwu Valley. All these routes cross rugged and perilous mountains. Order the troops to level the roads, repair the bridges, hew through mountains, and break apart rocks, allowing nothing to obstruct the march. Anyone who disobeys will be punished under military law.” Xu Yi accepted the command and advanced with his troops. Zhong Hui followed with more than a hundred thousand men, marching day and night.

p.src: Meanwhile, Deng Ai was in Longxi. Upon receiving the edict to attack Shu, he first ordered Sima Wang to hold the Qiang people in check. He also sent orders to Zhuge Xu, Inspector of Yongzhou; Wang Qi, Administrator of Tianshui; Qian Hong, Administrator of Longxi; and Yang Xin, Administrator of Jincheng, each to muster the troops under his command and come to receive orders. By the time the troops had gathered like clouds, Deng Ai dreamed one night that he had climbed a high mountain and was gazing toward Hanzhong when a spring suddenly burst forth beneath his feet, its waters surging upward. He awoke with a start, drenched in sweat, and sat waiting for dawn. Then he summoned his guard Shao Huan and asked him about it. Shao Huan had long been well versed in the Book of Changes. Deng Ai related his dream in full. Shao Huan replied, “The Changes says: ‘Water upon a mountain is called Jian, Obstruction. The hexagram Jian favors the southwest but not the northeast.’ Confucius said: ‘Jian favors the southwest. To go there brings achievement; it does not favor the northeast, for there the way comes to an end.’ On this campaign, General, you will certainly conquer Shu. Regrettably, however, obstruction will prevent your return.” Hearing this, Deng Ai grew somber and displeased. Just then Zhong Hui’s proclamation arrived, calling on Deng Ai to raise his army and rendezvous with him at Hanzhong. Deng Ai accordingly sent Zhuge Xu, Inspector of Yongzhou, with fifteen thousand troops to cut off Jiang Wei’s route of retreat. Next he sent Wang Qi, Administrator of Tianshui, with fifteen thousand troops to attack Tazhong from the left. Qian Hong, Administrator of Longxi, was to lead fifteen thousand troops against Tazhong from the right; and Yang Xin, Administrator of Jincheng, was sent with another fifteen thousand to intercept Jiang Wei’s rear at Gansong. Deng Ai himself led thirty thousand troops, moving to and fro to support the various forces.

p.src: When Zhong Hui’s army set out, all the officials escorted him beyond the city. Banners blotted out the sun, and armor gleamed like frost; the men were strong and the horses sturdy; their awe-inspiring might drew admiration from all who saw them. Only Liu Shi, an aide to the Chancellor of State, smiled faintly and said nothing. The Grand Commandant Wang Xiang saw Liu Shi’s cold smile. From horseback he took Liu Shi by the hand and asked, “Will Zhong Hui and Deng Ai be able to pacify Shu on this expedition?” Liu Shi said, “They will certainly destroy Shu, but I fear that neither will return to the capital.” Wang Xiang asked why, but Liu Shi merely smiled and did not answer. Wang Xiang therefore asked no more.

p.src: After the Wei armies had set out, a spy soon reached Tazhong and reported the news to Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei at once prepared a memorial to the Latter Ruler, requesting an edict ordering Zhang Yi, General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Left, to lead troops in defense of Yangping Pass, and Liao Hua, General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Right, to defend the Yinping Bridge: “These two places are of the utmost importance. If they are lost, Hanzhong cannot be held. At the same time, an envoy should be sent to Wu to seek aid. Meanwhile, I shall personally raise the troops at Tazhong to resist the enemy.” At this time the Latter Ruler had changed the fifth year of Jingyao to the first year of Yanxing, and spent every day amusing himself in the palace with the eunuch Huang Hao. On suddenly receiving Jiang Wei’s memorial, he summoned Huang Hao and asked, “Wei has now sent Zhong Hui and Deng Ai with great armies advancing by separate routes. What are we to do?” Huang Hao replied, “Jiang Wei merely wishes to win fame and merit, and that is why he has submitted this memorial. Set Your Majesty’s mind at ease and harbor no doubts or fears. I have heard that there is a shamaness in the city who serves a deity and can foretell good and ill fortune. She may be summoned and questioned.” The Latter Ruler followed his advice. In the rear hall he laid out incense, flowers, paper offerings, candles, and sacrificial gifts, then ordered Huang Hao to bring the shamaness into the palace in a small carriage and seat her upon the imperial couch. The Latter Ruler finished burning incense and offering his prayer. Suddenly the shamaness loosened her hair and bared her feet, leaped dozens of times around the hall, and whirled upon the altar table. Huang Hao said, “The divine spirit has descended. Your Majesty should dismiss the attendants and pray to it in person.” The Latter Ruler dismissed all his attendants, bowed twice, and prayed. The shamaness cried out, “I am the tutelary god of Xichuan. Your Majesty should delight in peace and tranquillity. Why inquire into other matters? Within a few years, the territory of Wei will also belong to Your Majesty. Your Majesty must not worry.” Having spoken, she collapsed unconscious upon the floor and did not revive until some time later. The Latter Ruler was overjoyed and rewarded her lavishly. From then on he firmly believed the shamaness’s words and paid no heed to Jiang Wei’s advice, but spent every day feasting and making merry in the palace. Jiang Wei repeatedly submitted urgent memorials, but Huang Hao concealed them all, and thus affairs of the greatest consequence were delayed.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zhong Hui’s great army advanced in a long column toward Hanzhong. Xu Yi, vanguard commander of the foremost division, was eager to win the first distinction and led his troops ahead to Nanzheng Pass. Xu Yi said to his officers, “Beyond this pass lies Hanzhong. There are few troops upon it; if we exert ourselves, we can seize the pass.” The officers obeyed and pressed forward together with all their strength. But the Shu general Lu Xun, who guarded the pass, had long known that the Wei army was coming. He had concealed soldiers on both sides of the wooden bridge before the pass and set up the repeating crossbows left by the Martial Marquis, each capable of firing ten bolts. Just as Xu Yi’s troops came to storm the pass, a wooden clapper sounded, and bolts and stones poured down like rain. Xu Yi hastily tried to withdraw. But dozens of horsemen had already been shot down. The Wei troops suffered a great defeat. Xu Yi returned and reported to Zhong Hui. Zhong Hui himself brought more than a hundred armored horsemen of his guard to inspect the place, and sure enough, bows and crossbows loosed upon them all at once. Zhong Hui wheeled his horse and retreated, whereupon Lu Xun led five hundred troops down from the pass in pursuit. Zhong Hui spurred across the bridge, but its earthen surface gave way and trapped his horse’s hoof, nearly pitching him from the saddle. The horse could not wrench itself free, so Zhong Hui abandoned it and fled on foot. As he ran off the bridge, Lu Xun caught up and thrust his spear at him, but Xun Kai of the Wei army turned and shot an arrow that knocked Lu Xun from his horse. Zhong Hui urged his men to seize the opportunity and storm the pass. Because Shu soldiers were still before the defenses, the troops atop the pass dared not shoot. Zhong Hui scattered them and captured the mountain pass. He then appointed Xun Kai Army Protector and rewarded him with a fully equipped horse and a suit of armor. Zhong Hui summoned Xu Yi before his tent and rebuked him: “As vanguard, it was your duty to open roads through mountains and lay bridges across waters, attending especially to the repair of bridges and roads so the army could march unhindered. Just now my horse’s hoof became trapped upon the bridge, and I nearly fell from it. Had it not been for Xun Kai, I would already have been slain! Since you have violated military orders, you shall be dealt with under military law!” He shouted for the attendants to drag Xu Yi out and behead him. The officers pleaded, “His father, Xu Chu, rendered great service to the court. We beg the commander to pardon him.” Zhong Hui angrily replied, “If military law is not clearly enforced, how can the troops be commanded?” He therefore ordered Xu Yi beheaded as a warning to all. Every officer was appalled.

p.src: At that time, the Shu general Wang Han guarded Lecheng, while Jiang Bin guarded Hancheng. Seeing the overwhelming strength of the Wei army, they dared not offer battle and merely shut their gates and held their defenses. Zhong Hui issued an order: “In war, divine speed is prized; we must not halt even briefly.” He ordered Li Fu of the vanguard to besiege Lecheng and Army Protector Xun Kai to besiege Hancheng, while he led the main army against Yangping Pass. The Shu general Fu Qian, who guarded the pass, consulted his deputy Jiang Shu on whether to fight or defend. Jiang Shu said, “The Wei troops are exceedingly numerous and their power cannot be withstood. Our best course is to hold fast.” Fu Qian replied, “That is not so. The Wei troops have come from afar and must be weary. Though they are many, they need not be feared. If we do not descend from the pass and fight, Hancheng and Lecheng will be lost.” Jiang Shu remained silent and made no reply. Suddenly word came that the main body of the Wei army had reached the pass, and Jiang Shu and Fu Qian went atop the defenses to look. Zhong Hui raised his whip and shouted, “I have now brought an army of one hundred thousand here. If you surrender at once, each of you shall be promoted and employed according to rank. But if you stubbornly refuse, once the pass is breached, jade and stone alike shall be burned!” Fu Qian flew into a rage. Ordering Jiang Shu to hold the pass, he personally led three thousand troops down to attack. Zhong Hui at once fled, and all the Wei troops retreated. Fu Qian pursued his advantage, whereupon the Wei forces closed ranks again. When Fu Qian sought to withdraw into the pass, the banners of Wei had already been raised above it. Then Jiang Shu called out, “I have surrendered to Wei!” Fu Qian raged and fiercely cursed him: “You ungrateful, faithless traitor! With what face can you meet the Son of Heaven?” He wheeled his horse and once more engaged the Wei troops. The Wei troops converged from every side and surrounded Fu Qian at the heart of the battlefield. Fu Qian charged left and right, fighting desperately back and forth, but could not break free. Of the Shu troops under him, eight or nine in ten were wounded or slain. Fu Qian looked up to Heaven and sighed: “In life I am a minister of Shu; in death I shall be a ghost of Shu!” Then he spurred his horse into the fray once more. Pierced by several spears, his robe and armor drenched in blood, he fell when his mount collapsed beneath him; Fu Qian cut his own throat and died. A later poet lamented him in these lines:

p.src: Zhong Hui captured Yangping Pass and found vast stores of grain, fodder, and weapons within. Overjoyed, he rewarded the whole army. That night the Wei troops lodged in Yang’an, when suddenly tremendous battle cries arose to the southwest. Zhong Hui hurried from his tent to look, but there was no sign of anything. The Wei army dared not sleep all night. On the following night, during the second watch, the cries again arose in the southwest. Alarmed and perplexed, Zhong Hui sent men to investigate toward dawn. They returned and reported, “We scouted more than ten li into the distance and found not a single person.” Still filled with uncertainty, Zhong Hui personally led several hundred fully armed and equipped horsemen on patrol toward the southwest. They came to a mountain and saw a murderous aura suddenly rising on every side, as sorrowful clouds gathered and mist locked the summit. Zhong Hui reined in his horse and asked the local guide, “What mountain is this?” The guide replied, “This is Mount Dingjun, where Xiahou Yuan met his death in former days.” Hearing this, Zhong Hui grew melancholy and uneasy, and turned his horse back. As they rounded the mountain slope, a furious wind suddenly arose, and several thousand horsemen burst out behind them, charging with the gale. Zhong Hui was greatly alarmed and led his men galloping away. Countless officers fell from their horses. Yet when they reached Yangping Pass, not a single man or horse had been lost; they had only bruised their faces in falls and lost their helmets. They all said, “We saw men and horses charging from within the dark clouds, but when they came close, they harmed no one; it was only a whirlwind.” Zhong Hui asked the surrendered general Jiang Shu, “Is there a shrine to some deity on Mount Dingjun?” Jiang Shu replied, “There is no shrine there, only the tomb of Zhuge, the Martial Marquis.” Zhong Hui exclaimed in astonishment, “This must have been a manifestation of the Martial Marquis’s spirit. I must go in person and offer sacrifice to him.”

p.src: The next day, Zhong Hui prepared sacrificial offerings, slaughtered the full complement of ox, sheep, and pig, and went in person to the Martial Marquis’s tomb, where he bowed twice and performed the rites. When the rites were finished, the furious wind at once subsided and the sorrowful clouds scattered in every direction. Suddenly a fresh breeze softly stirred, and a fine rain began to fall. After this brief shower, the sky became bright and clear. The Wei troops rejoiced greatly; all bowed in thanks and returned to camp. That night, Zhong Hui fell asleep leaning over a low table in his tent. Suddenly a fresh breeze passed through, and there appeared a man wearing a silk headcloth and carrying a feather fan. He was clad in a crane-feather cloak, with plain shoes and a black sash; his face was fair as polished jade, his lips red as vermilion, his brows fine and his eyes bright. He stood eight feet tall and bore the ethereal air of an immortal. The man stepped into the tent. Zhong Hui rose to receive him and asked, “Who are you, sir?” The man replied, “This morning you graciously honored me with a visit, and I have a few words to tell you. Though the fortune of Han is already in decline and Heaven’s mandate cannot be defied, it is truly pitiable that the common people of the Two Rivers should be visited by the calamity of war without cause. After entering their land, you must on no account wantonly slaughter its people.” Having spoken, he swept his sleeves and departed. Zhong Hui tried to detain him, but suddenly awoke and realized it had been a dream. He knew it had been the spirit of the Martial Marquis and was filled with astonishment and awe. He therefore sent an order to the vanguard to raise a white banner bearing the four characters, “Protect the Realm and Pacify the People.” Wherever the army went, anyone who wantonly killed even one person would pay with his life. Thereupon all the people of Hanzhong came out of their towns and bowed in welcome. Zhong Hui reassured them one by one, and his troops did not take so much as an autumn hare’s down. u.src: The next day, Zhong Hui prepared sacrificial offerings, slaughtered the full complement of ox, sheep, and pig, and went in person to the Martial Marquis’s tomb, where he bowed twice and performed the rites.
When the rites were finished, the furious wind at once subsided and the sorrowful clouds scattered in every direction.
Suddenly a fresh breeze softly stirred, and a fine rain began to fall.
After this brief shower, the sky became bright and clear.
The Wei troops rejoiced greatly; all bowed in thanks and returned to camp.

p.src: Now Jiang Wei, while at Tazhong, learned that the Wei army was approaching in great force and sent dispatches ordering Liao Hua, Zhang Yi, and Dong Jue to bring troops to his support; meanwhile, he divided his own forces and arrayed his commanders to await the enemy. Suddenly a report came that the Wei troops had arrived. Jiang Wei led his troops out to meet them. The foremost commander in the Wei ranks was Wang Qi, Administrator of Tianshui. Wang Qi rode forward and cried aloud, “We now have a million troops and a thousand great commanders, advancing by twenty separate routes; they have already reached Chengdu. Why do you not think of surrendering at once? You still seek to resist—can you not recognize Heaven’s decree?” Jiang Wei flew into a rage, leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and charged straight at Wang Qi. They had fought fewer than three bouts when Wang Qi was soundly defeated and fled. Jiang Wei drove his troops in pursuit, cutting down the enemy for twenty li, when suddenly gongs and drums sounded together and a body of troops deployed before him; upon its banner were written in large characters: “Qian Hong, Administrator of Longxi.” Jiang Wei laughed. “Such rats are no match for me!” He then urged his troops onward in pursuit. After another ten li, he encountered Deng Ai leading troops against him. The two armies became locked in a confused battle. Jiang Wei roused all his valor and fought Deng Ai for more than ten bouts without either gaining the advantage; then gongs and drums sounded again behind him. As Jiang Wei hurriedly withdrew, his rearguard reported, “All the camps at Gansong have been burned down by Yang Xin, Administrator of Jincheng.” Jiang Wei was greatly alarmed. He at once ordered a deputy commander to display false banners and hold Deng Ai at bay, while he himself withdrew the rear division and hastened through the night to save Gansong, where he came face-to-face with Yang Xin. Yang Xin dared not engage him and fled toward the mountain road. Jiang Wei pursued close behind. As he neared the foot of the cliffs, timber and stones rained down from above, and Jiang Wei could advance no farther. By the time he had turned back and reached the middle of the road, Deng Ai had already routed the Shu troops. The main Wei army came on and surrounded Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei led his cavalry in cutting their way out through the encirclement, then hurried into the main camp and held it firmly while awaiting reinforcements. Suddenly an express rider arrived and reported, “Zhong Hui has broken through Yangping Pass. Its defending commander Jiang Shu has surrendered, Fu Qian has died in battle, and Hanzhong now belongs to Wei. Wang Han, commander of Lecheng, and Jiang Bin, commander of Hancheng, learned that Hanzhong was lost and likewise opened their gates and surrendered. Hu Ji could not withstand the enemy and has fled back to Chengdu to seek aid.”

p.src: Jiang Wei was greatly alarmed and immediately ordered the camp struck. That night his army reached the mouth of Jiangchuan, where a force was drawn up ahead. The Wei commander at its head was Yang Xin, Administrator of Jincheng. Jiang Wei flew into a rage and spurred forward to engage him. After a single bout Yang Xin fled in defeat, and Jiang Wei took up his bow and shot at him; but all three arrows missed. Jiang Wei turned his anger upon the bow and snapped it in two, then leveled his spear and gave chase. His warhorse stumbled with its forelegs, throwing him to the ground, and Yang Xin wheeled his horse around to kill him. Jiang Wei sprang to his feet and thrust with his spear, striking Yang Xin’s horse squarely in the head. Wei troops rushed up from behind and carried Yang Xin away to safety. Jiang Wei mounted a warhorse and was about to pursue when a sudden report came that Deng Ai’s troops had arrived behind him. Unable to attend to both front and rear, Jiang Wei gathered his troops and resolved to retake Hanzhong. A scout reported, “Zhuge Xu, Inspector of Yongzhou, has cut off our road of retreat.” Jiang Wei encamped upon a defensible mountain position. The Wei troops were stationed at the head of Yinping Bridge. With no road either forward or back, Jiang Wei sighed deeply. “Heaven means to destroy me!” His deputy Ning Sui said, “Though the Wei army has cut off Yinping Bridge, Yongzhou must now be thinly defended. If you march through Konghan Valley and make straight for Yongzhou, Zhuge Xu will surely withdraw his forces from Yinping to save it. You may then lead our troops to Jiange and hold it, and Hanzhong can be recovered.” Jiang Wei followed this counsel, immediately sending his troops into Konghan Valley and feigning an attack on Yongzhou. A spy reported this to Zhuge Xu. Zhuge Xu was greatly alarmed. “Yongzhou is the place where my forces are to assemble. If I should let it be lost through negligence, the court will certainly hold me to account.” He hurriedly withdrew the main army and took the southern road to relieve Yongzhou, leaving only one detachment to guard the bridgehead. Jiang Wei entered the northern road and traveled about thirty li. Judging that the Wei army must by then have set out, he wheeled his troops around, made the rear division the vanguard, and went straight to the bridgehead. As expected, the main Wei force had gone, leaving only a few soldiers on guard, whom Jiang Wei scattered in a single onslaught. He burned all their camps and palisades. When Zhuge Xu learned that fire had broken out at the bridgehead, he led his troops back again. But Jiang Wei’s army had already been gone for half a day, so he dared not pursue.

p.src: Now Jiang Wei led his troops across the bridgehead. As they marched, an army approached from ahead, commanded by Zhang Yi, General of the Left, and Liao Hua, General of the Right. Jiang Wei asked them what had happened. Zhang Yi said, “Huang Hao trusted the words of a sorcerer and refused to send troops. When I heard that Hanzhong was in danger, I raised troops and came of my own accord, but by then Yangping Pass had already been taken by Zhong Hui. Now, hearing that you were hard pressed, General, we came especially to your aid.” Thereupon they joined their forces into one. Liao Hua said, “We are now beset by enemies on every side and our supply route is cut. It would be better to retreat and hold Jiange, then devise a sound plan.” Jiang Wei hesitated, unable to decide. Suddenly word came that Zhong Hui and Deng Ai had divided their forces into more than ten columns and were attacking. Jiang Wei wished to divide the troops with Zhang Yi and Liao Hua and meet them in battle. Liao Hua said, “Baishui is narrow and crossed by many roads; it is no place to contend in battle. Better to withdraw for now and go to the relief of Jiange. If Jiange should once be lost, our road will be cut off.” Jiang Wei followed his counsel and led the army toward Jiange.
